name: Sertraline (Zoloft)
summary: SSRI antidepressant used for depression, panic, OCD, PTSD, social anxiety, and PMDD. Usually takes a few weeks to feel a real shift, and it’s not physically addictive—but stopping abruptly can still feel rough.
description: Sertraline is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI). It’s commonly prescribed for depression and anxiety-spectrum conditions like panic disorder, OCD, PTSD, and social anxiety. The first 1–2 weeks are often about side effects (nausea, jittery energy, insomnia). The “this is actually helping” part usually builds over 4–6 weeks, and sometimes longer for OCD/PTSD. There’s a boxed warning about increased suicidal thoughts/behavior in people under 25 in short-term studies—so early monitoring matters. Don’t mix with MAOIs, and watch for serotonin syndrome if you combine serotonergic meds.
patient_summary: Sertraline (Zoloft) is an SSRI used for depression, panic, OCD, PTSD, social anxiety, and PMDD. It usually takes weeks—not hours—to work. Early side effects like nausea, diarrhea, insomnia, or feeling “activated” can show up before benefits. There’s a known increased risk of suicidal thoughts/behavior in people under 25 early in treatment, so close follow-up is important. Not physically addictive, but you still want a gradual taper to avoid withdrawal symptoms.

primary_indications: Panic Disorder (with or without agoraphobia) in adults

linked_conditions.context: A core SSRI option for unipolar depression. Expect early side effects first; mood and motivation improvements usually build over weeks.
One of the go-to SSRIs for OCD. OCD often needs a longer trial and higher end dosing compared to depression.
Effective for panic attacks and anticipatory anxiety. Starting low helps reduce early jitteriness that can mimic panic.
A first-line SSRI option for PTSD symptoms. Benefits can take several weeks and may continue building for 8–12 weeks.
Helpful for persistent social anxiety (not just performance moments). Usually needs steady daily dosing and patience.
Can be used daily or intermittently (luteal-phase or symptom-onset dosing). Some people feel improvement within the first cycle.
Common off-label SSRI option for chronic worry/tension. Slow titration helps if you’re sensitive to activation.
Often treated with SSRI-style dosing strategies, sometimes requiring higher doses and longer trials for full effect.
Sometimes used when binge/purge symptoms are prominent and mood/anxiety are part of the picture.
May reduce binge frequency in some patients; dosing is typically similar to depression-range dosing.

contraindications: Concurrent use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs), including methylene blue, or use within 14 days of stopping an MAOI or sertraline
Hypersensitivity to sertraline or any component of the formulation (eg, anaphylaxis, angioedema)
Concurrent use with disulfiram (oral solution only)

efficacy_response.patient_text: Sertraline doesn’t work like a rescue med. Many people notice small shifts (less edge, fewer spirals, slightly easier mornings) within 1–2 weeks, but the stronger, steadier benefits usually build over 4–6 weeks. OCD and PTSD often take longer—sometimes up to 12 weeks for a fair trial.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Oral absorption with measurable plasma levels after dosing
pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: Tablets and oral solution considered equivalent
pharmacokinetics.onset: Depression: initial effects may appear within 1–2 weeks; anxiety-spectrum conditions often show early changes around 2 weeks with continued improvement through 4–6 weeks (sometimes longer for OCD/PTSD)
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Sertraline ~26 hours (average); active metabolite (N-desmethylsertraline) ~62 to 104 hours
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Once-daily dosing due to half-life and steady-state pharmacology
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic metabolism (multiple CYP pathways; clinically relevant interaction potential with CYP inducers/inhibitors)
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Urine and feces primarily as metabolites
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Can be taken with or without food; choose a consistent routine if GI side effects are an issue

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Sertraline (Zoloft) is an SSRI—meaning it’s a daily medication that gradually reduces symptoms over weeks. In psychiatry, it’s used for depression and several anxiety-spectrum conditions, including panic disorder, OCD, PTSD, social anxiety, and PMDD.
items: {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)}: Low mood, low interest, low energy, negative thinking patterns
{link:condition:obsessive-compulsive-disorder:Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)}: Intrusive thoughts + compulsive behaviors that feel hard to resist
{link:condition:panic-disorder:Panic Disorder}: Panic attacks and fear of the next one
{link:condition:posttraumatic-stress-disorder:PTSD}: Re-experiencing, hypervigilance, avoidance, and mood symptoms after trauma
{link:condition:social-anxiety-disorder:Social Anxiety Disorder}: Fear of judgment, avoidance, physical anxiety in social situations
{link:condition:premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder:PMDD}: Severe mood symptoms tied to the menstrual cycle

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: This is the real-world pattern people describe most often—especially in the first month:

quotes: I felt weirdly jittery, like I had caffeine anxiety.
My stomach was not impressed. Nausea and diarrhea for a bit.
Sleep got choppy at first—even though I was exhausted.
items.note: Early GI symptoms and activation (restlessness, insomnia, increased anxiety) are common. Starting low and titrating slowly can help.

quotes: I didn’t feel ‘happy,’ but I felt less stuck.
The spirals didn’t grab me as hard.
Panic sensations softened—like the volume turned down.
items.note: Some people notice early improvement; others need more time. OCD/PTSD often take longer.

quotes: It wasn’t dramatic, but I felt more like myself again.
My mood didn’t crash as easily.
I could do the things I knew were good for me again.
My libido dropped and it was frustrating.
Orgasms took longer or didn’t happen sometimes.
Everything worked, it just felt… muted.
items.note: Sexual dysfunction can be dose-related and persistent. It’s common enough that it should be discussed upfront.

quotes: I felt more agitated than depressed, which scared me.
My thoughts got darker out of nowhere.
I needed closer check-ins the first few weeks.
items.note: Antidepressants can increase suicidal thoughts/behavior in pediatric and young adult patients in short-term studies. Close monitoring early on is essential.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Sertraline is not an instant-relief medication. Think “slow build,” not “quick hit.”
key_points: First few days: side effects may show up before benefits (GI upset, insomnia, jittery energy)
1–2 weeks: some people notice early shifts (less panic intensity, slightly better mood, fewer intrusive spikes)
4–6 weeks: typical window for clearer antidepressant/anxiolytic effect
8–12 weeks: a fair trial for tougher targets like OCD/PTSD (and sometimes body dysmorphic symptoms)
Once daily: sertraline is taken daily because it’s designed for steady blood levels, not PRN use

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.value: 4–6 weeks for many conditions; up to 12 weeks for OCD/PTSD in some patients
sections.text: Sertraline is widely used because it can reduce both emotional symptoms (sadness, fear, intrusive thoughts) and physical symptoms (panic sensations, tension, hypervigilance). The catch is timing: you usually have to stay consistent long enough for the medication to actually do its job.
sections.clinical_details: Many patients experience early side effects that fade over 1–2 weeks, while benefits build gradually over 4–6 weeks. OCD and PTSD often need longer trials and sometimes higher-end doses before response is obvious. For PMDD, some patients respond within the first menstrual cycle, especially with symptom-linked dosing strategies.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: If you’re under 25, early monitoring matters: antidepressants can increase suicidal thoughts/behavior in short-term studies.
sections.black_box: Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in pediatric and young adult patients in short-term studies. Closely monitor all antidepressant-treated patients for clinical worsening, and for emergence of suicidal thoughts and behaviors.
other: Serotonin syndrome risk—especially if combined with other serotonergic meds (or overdose): agitation, confusion, tremor, rigidity, fever, diarrhea, rapid heart rate
Activation of mania/hypomania: antidepressants can trigger mood switching, especially in undiagnosed bipolar disorder
Bleeding risk: SSRIs can increase bleeding risk, especially with NSAIDs, antiplatelets, or anticoagulants
Hyponatremia/SIADH risk: higher risk in older adults, low body weight, diuretic use, or prior low sodium
Angle-closure glaucoma risk in susceptible patients (rare but urgent)
QT prolongation and torsades have been reported (typically with other risk factors)
patient_counseling: If you feel suddenly worse, more agitated, more impulsive, or develop suicidal thoughts—call your prescriber right away. If you’re in danger, go to the ER or call emergency services.
If you have any history of bipolar disorder (or strong family history), tell your clinician before starting. New insomnia + racing thoughts + risky behavior can be a red flag.
Don’t combine with MAOIs. Keep the 14-day washout rules both directions.
If you’re on blood thinners or take frequent NSAIDs (like ibuprofen/naproxen), ask about bleeding risk and warning signs (easy bruising, black stools, unusual bleeding).
If you’re older or at risk for low sodium, sodium checks may be part of your early monitoring—especially after dose changes.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: GI side effects (nausea, diarrhea), insomnia or activation early on, fatigue or drowsiness in some, tremor, and sexual dysfunction. Many side effects improve over time, but sexual side effects can persist.
plain_language_list: Sexual side effects (lower libido, delayed orgasm, erectile issues)
Sweating, appetite changes, weight changes over time

common.patient_note: Usually shows up early and often fades within 1–2 weeks. Taking it with food or switching dosing time can help.
Common early SSRI side effect. Hydration matters. If severe or persistent, dose adjustments or a slower titration can help.
Often worse early. Taking sertraline in the morning can help if it’s activating; some people do better at night if it makes them sleepy.
Some people feel sluggish early; this can improve. If fatigue persists, timing changes or dose adjustments may help.
Less common than insomnia, but it happens. Don’t drive or operate machinery if you feel impaired until you know your baseline.
Can happen during initiation or dose increases. Rising slowly and hydration can help.
Often mild but annoying. Can be dose-related.
This can feel like anxiety got worse. Starting at 12.5–25 mg and titrating slowly is often the fix.
Decreased libido, delayed orgasm, erectile dysfunction, or orgasm disruption can occur. It’s a real quality-of-life issue—bring it up early so you have options.

serious: Serotonin syndrome: agitation, confusion, hyperreflexia, rigidity, fever, sweating, diarrhea, rapid heart rate. MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Suicidal thinking/behavior in pediatric and young adult patients in short-term studies: monitor closely, especially during the first 1–2 months or dose changes.
Mania/hypomania: decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, impulsive behavior, grandiosity—especially if bipolar disorder is present or unrecognized.
Severe hyponatremia/SIADH: confusion, headache, weakness, seizures (higher risk in older adults and with diuretics).
Serious skin reactions (rare): SJS/TEN or other severe rashes—stop and seek urgent care if rash is severe, blistering, or involves mucous membranes.
Significant bleeding: especially with anticoagulants/antiplatelets/NSAIDs (black stools, vomiting blood, unexplained bruising).
QT prolongation/torsades (rare): typically with other risk factors or interacting meds.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Sertraline has meaningful interactions mostly through serotonin effects (serotonin syndrome risk) and bleeding risk. Some combinations are flat-out contraindicated.

items.risk: Contraindicated. High risk of serious serotonin toxicity and dangerous reactions.
items.action: Allow 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting sertraline, and 14 days between stopping sertraline and starting an MAOI.

items.risk: Contraindicated. Increased risk of serious cardiac effects (including QT-related risks).

items.with: Other serotonergic meds (other SSRIs/SNRIs, triptans, tramadol, linezolid, lithium, St. John’s wort, MDMA, some migraine meds)
items.risk: Serotonin syndrome risk (can be rapid and severe).
items.action: Use caution, avoid unnecessary stacking, and educate patients on warning signs (agitation, confusion, tremor, rigidity, fever, diarrhea).

items.risk: Higher bleeding risk (bruising, GI bleed, intracranial bleed—rare but serious).
items.action: Use with caution, monitor, and minimize avoidable NSAID use when possible.

items.risk: Not a classic “don’t ever” like benzos + alcohol, but alcohol can worsen depression/anxiety and amplify sedation or impairment in some people.
items.action: If you drink, keep it minimal and pay attention to mood, sleep, and impulsivity.
Use tablets/capsules instead, or choose a different antidepressant plan.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Sertraline isn’t physically addictive, but stopping suddenly can still trigger a withdrawal-like discontinuation syndrome—especially after 4+ weeks of use. The safest move is a gradual taper so your brain has time to adapt.
key_points: Typical taper: over 2–4 weeks for many patients after ≥4 weeks of treatment; longer tapers may be needed for higher doses, prior withdrawal history, or long-term treatment
Short courses: 2–3 weeks of treatment may taper over 1–2 weeks; <2 weeks often doesn’t require tapering (but individual sensitivity varies)
If withdrawal symptoms hit hard: resume the prior dose and taper more slowly
Common discontinuation symptoms: dizziness, “electric shock” sensations, nausea, chills, headache, irritability, anxiety, insomnia
Sertraline capsules: doses below 150 mg require switching to another sertraline formulation for tapering (capsules are 150 mg and 200 mg)

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Sertraline is usually taken once daily. Most people do best starting low (especially if you’re anxiety-sensitive) and increasing gradually. The goal is a dose that actually treats the condition—not just a starter dose you stay stuck on.

adult.mdd_titration: Increase by 25–50 mg/day no more than once weekly based on response and tolerability
adult.mdd_max: 200 mg/day (labeling); some clinical practice uses up to 300 mg/day with specialist oversight
adult.ocd_titration: Increase by 25–50 mg/day no more than once weekly based on response and tolerability
adult.ocd_max: 200 mg/day (labeling); some patients with inadequate response may benefit from doses up to 400 mg/day, but adverse effects may increase
adult.panic_initial: 25 mg PO once daily for 3–7 days, then increase to 50 mg/day
adult.panic_titration: Increase by 25–50 mg at intervals of at least 1 week based on response and tolerability
adult.ptsd_titration: Increase by 25–50 mg at intervals of at least 1 week based on response and tolerability
adult.ptsd_max: 200 mg/day (labeling); some clinical practice uses up to 250 mg/day
adult.social_anxiety_titration: After 4–6 weeks at a lower dose, increase by 25–50 mg at intervals of at least 1 week as needed
adult.social_anxiety_max: 200 mg/day (labeling); some clinical practice uses up to 250 mg/day
adult.pmdd_continuous_initial: 25 mg PO once daily; increase to 50 mg/day over the first month as needed
adult.pmdd_luteal_phase_initial: 25 mg PO once daily during luteal phase only (start 14 days before expected menses; stop at onset of menses); may increase to 50 mg/day over the first month
adult.pmdd_symptom_onset_initial: 25 mg PO once daily starting on the day symptoms begin and continue until a few days after menses starts; may increase to 50 mg/day over the first month
adult.gad_titration: Increase by 25–50 mg/day at intervals of at least 1 week based on response and tolerability (in inpatient settings, may increase every 3–4 days if warranted)
adult.binge_eating_initial: 25 mg PO once daily after lunch
adult.binge_eating_titration: Increase by 25 mg every 3 days based on response and tolerability (some experts prefer slower titration of at least 1 week)
adult.bdd_titration: Increase by 50 mg at intervals of every 2–3 weeks based on response and tolerability
adult.bdd_typical: 200 mg/day (often requires a 12–16 week trial; if using 200 mg, consider at least 4 weeks at 200 mg before judging response)
adult.bdd_max: Some patients may require up to 400 mg/day if tolerated (specialist-level dosing due to adverse effect risk)
adult.bulimia_titration: Increase by 50 mg at intervals of at least 1 week based on response and tolerability
adult.premature_ejaculation_daily: 50 mg PO once daily; increase by 50 mg about every 3–4 weeks as needed up to 200 mg/day
adult.premature_ejaculation_on_demand: 100 mg PO 6–8 hours before intercourse; maximum twice weekly with at least 3 days between doses
adult.capsule_use_note: Do not initiate treatment with capsules. Use tablets or oral solution for initiation and titration and for doses under 150 mg/day. Capsules (150 mg or 200 mg) may be considered only after a patient has been stable on 100–125 mg/day for at least 1 week or on at least 150 mg/day.

sections.simple_explanation: Start low if you’re sensitive (especially with anxiety/panic), then increase slowly. With SSRIs, the goal is a steady daily dose that builds benefit over weeks. If early activation shows up, the fix is often a slower titration—not giving up immediately.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Sertraline is one of the most commonly used SSRIs in pregnancy and breastfeeding when treatment is needed. The right decision depends on illness severity, relapse history, and shared decision-making—not fear-based stopping.
sections.pregnancy: Evaluate pregnancy status before starting when relevant. SSRIs as a class have extensive pregnancy data; overall, a clear increased risk of major congenital malformations has not been consistently observed for sertraline across studies, though results can vary by design and confounders. Late pregnancy SSRI exposure can be associated with neonatal adaptation syndrome (usually resolves within ~2 weeks) and a rare risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN). Reducing or stopping an effective SSRI right before delivery is not recommended solely to reduce neonatal symptoms. Untreated or undertreated depression/anxiety/PTSD/OCD can also worsen pregnancy outcomes, so treatment decisions should be individualized and collaborative.
sections.lactation: Sertraline is present in breast milk, but infant exposure is generally low (relative infant dose typically well below thresholds commonly considered acceptable). Sertraline is often a preferred SSRI in breastfeeding when an antidepressant is needed. Monitor the infant for irritability, feeding changes, sleep changes, and growth/development.
sections.pediatrics: Psychiatry-focused pediatric use includes OCD and sometimes depression (depending on clinical context). Children may be more prone to behavioral activation (restlessness/hyperactivity/agitation). Start low and titrate slowly, and monitor growth (weight/height/BMI) over time.
sections.geriatrics: Use with caution in older adults due to higher risk of hyponatremia/SIADH and falls (especially if there’s a history of recurrent falls). Lower starting doses (often 25 mg/day) may be better tolerated. Consider checking sodium after initiation and dose changes.
sections.hepatic: Hepatic impairment increases exposure and prolongs half-life. In cirrhosis (Child-Turcotte-Pugh A or B), use 50% of the usual indication-specific dose and increase slowly in small increments (≤25 mg) at intervals of at least 2 weeks; maximum often limited to 100 mg/day in this context. Child-Turcotte-Pugh C: use is not recommended. Sertraline capsules are not recommended in liver impairment because you can’t adjust dose flexibly.
sections.renal: Mild to severe renal impairment: no dosage adjustment typically necessary; sertraline is not dialyzable and does not require dialysis-related adjustments.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Suicidality and clinical worsening: especially during the first 1–2 months and during dose increases/decreases, with extra attention for patients under 25
Activation symptoms: anxiety, agitation, insomnia, irritability, impulsivity, akathisia—these can look like ‘it’s making me worse’ and may require dose/time adjustments or slower titration
Mania/hypomania screening: new decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, risky behavior, grandiosity—especially if bipolar disorder is possible
Serum sodium in at-risk patients (older adults, diuretic use, low baseline sodium, low body weight, prior hyponatremia), particularly after initiation or dose adjustments
Bleeding risk: bruising, GI bleeding symptoms, and interactions if taking NSAIDs, antiplatelets, or anticoagulants
Weight/height/BMI over time (especially in pediatrics); appetite/weight trends in adults during longer treatment
Sexual function and relationship impact: track it, don’t ignore it
Symptom scales when possible: PHQ-9 for depression; GAD-7 for anxiety; panic tracking; OCD symptom measures; PTSD check-ins
Adherence and timing: consistent daily dosing is a big part of whether SSRIs work

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Sertraline comes in multiple oral forms. The key practical detail: capsules are not for starting or fine-tuning early doses.
items: Oral concentrate solution: 20 mg/mL (must be diluted before use; direct undiluted dosing can numb the mouth and tastes astringent)
Capsules: 150 mg, 200 mg (do not use to initiate treatment; swallow whole—do not open, crush, or chew)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Sertraline is an SSRI. It selectively blocks presynaptic serotonin (5-HT) reuptake, which increases serotonin signaling over time. It has very weak effects on norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake and does not meaningfully bind many other receptor families—one reason it’s widely used and generally well tolerated (even though side effects still happen).

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Sertraline is a classic first-line medication across multiple psychiatric conditions: depression, panic disorder, OCD, PTSD, social anxiety, and PMDD. It’s a “foundation” med—best when taken consistently and given enough time at a therapeutic dose. For panic/anxiety-sensitive patients, starting low (12.5–25 mg) and titrating slowly can prevent early activation from derailing treatment. For OCD and related conditions, higher doses and longer trials are often necessary. Medication works best when paired with skills-based therapy (CBT, exposure/response prevention for OCD, trauma-focused therapy for PTSD) and lifestyle supports.

seo.title: Sertraline (Zoloft): Uses, Dosage, Side Effects, Warnings & Tapering
seo.description: Sertraline (Zoloft) is an SSRI for depression, panic disorder, OCD, PTSD, social anxiety, and PMDD. Learn dosing, how long it takes to work, common side effects (GI, insomnia, sexual), key interactions, boxed warning, and safe tapering.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Sertraline is an SSRI used for major depression, OCD, panic disorder, PTSD, social anxiety disorder, and PMDD. Clinicians also use it off-label for GAD, body dysmorphic disorder, binge eating disorder, bulimia nervosa, and sometimes premature ejaculation.

faqs.q: How long does sertraline take to work?
faqs.a: Some people notice small improvements in 1–2 weeks, but the more reliable benefit usually builds over 4–6 weeks. OCD and PTSD often need longer trials—sometimes up to 8–12 weeks—especially if higher doses are needed.

faqs.q: Why do I feel worse when starting sertraline?
faqs.a: Early “activation” can happen: jittery anxiety, restlessness, insomnia, irritability, or feeling wired. It can show up before benefits kick in. Starting at a lower dose (like 12.5–25 mg) and titrating slowly often reduces this problem.

Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in pediatric and young adult patients in short-term studies. That doesn’t mean it happens to everyone—but it does mean you deserve close follow-up early in treatment, especially if you’re under 25 or have a history of suicidality.

Yes—antidepressants can trigger mania or hypomania, especially if someone has bipolar disorder that hasn’t been identified yet. If you develop decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, impulsive/risky behavior, or unusually elevated/irritable mood, contact your prescriber quickly.

faqs.q: What are the most common sertraline side effects?
faqs.a: The big ones are GI symptoms (nausea, diarrhea), insomnia or jittery activation early on, fatigue or drowsiness in some people, tremor, sweating, and sexual side effects (lower libido, delayed orgasm, erectile issues). Many side effects improve within 1–2 weeks—sexual side effects are the one that can stick around.

Yes. SSRIs commonly cause decreased libido, delayed orgasm, orgasm difficulty, or erectile dysfunction. It can be dose-related and sometimes persists. If it’s affecting your life, tell your clinician—there are strategies to address it.

faqs.q: Do I need to taper sertraline?
faqs.a: If you’ve been on it for 4+ weeks, usually yes. Stopping abruptly can cause discontinuation symptoms like dizziness, nausea, irritability, anxiety, insomnia, and “electric shock” sensations. A gradual taper over 2–4 weeks is common, and longer tapers may be needed for higher doses or long-term treatment.

faqs.q: What medications should never be combined with sertraline?
faqs.a: Sertraline should not be combined with MAO inhibitors (including methylene blue) and should not be used with pimozide. You also need to be cautious stacking multiple serotonergic medications due to serotonin syndrome risk.

faqs.q: Is sertraline safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Sertraline is commonly used when treatment is needed in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and it’s often considered a preferred SSRI in breastfeeding due to generally low infant exposure. Late pregnancy exposure can be associated with neonatal adaptation symptoms and a rare risk of PPHN. The decision should be individualized with shared decision-making, balancing risks of medication with risks of untreated illness.

faqs.q: What’s the difference between sertraline tablets and capsules?
faqs.a: Capsules come in 150 mg and 200 mg strengths and should not be used to start sertraline or for early titration. For starting, dose changes, and doses under 150 mg/day, tablets or oral solution are used. Capsules are typically considered only after someone has been stable on certain tablet doses for at least a week.

faqs.q: Can sertraline be used for insomnia?
faqs.a: Sertraline isn’t an insomnia medication. It can improve sleep if depression or anxiety is driving the insomnia—but it can also cause insomnia (especially early) or, in some people, drowsiness. If sleep is the main issue, dosing time adjustments and sleep-focused strategies are usually part of the plan.
